#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ECI filing and waiver requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. For the stated FYE of 30/06/2026, the three-month ECI filing deadline is 30/09/2026, unless a filing exception applies. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company falls within 1 of the following categories, it does not need to file ECI: • Foreign ship owners or charterers whose local shipping agent has submitted/ will submit the Shipping Return (PDF, 104KB) • Foreign universities • Designated unit trusts and approved CPF unit trusts# • Real estate investment trusts that have been granted the tax treatment under Section 43(2) of the Income Tax Act 1947 • Cases specifically granted the waiver to furnish ECI by IRAS
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): If your company's ECI is nil and its annual revenue is more than $5 million, you are still required to file the ECI.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on staff medical expenses** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS states that staff medical input tax is generally disallowed under regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. Subject to the ordinary input-tax conditions, the stated exceptions are expenses obligatory under WICA or a qualifying Industrial Relations Act collective agreement; or, for expenses incurred on or after 1 October 2021, treatment connected with a work-related health risk or requirement and required under relevant Singapore written law. IRAS specifically says Primary Care Plan expenses do not meet the described work-related exception. A claim needs the expense date, legal/collective-agreement basis, work-related risk and mandate evidence, GST registration and invoice facts. #### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Corporate income tax treatment of approved donations** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** Donations are non-deductible expenses in arriving at adjusted profit. For donations made from 1 January 2016 through 31 December 2029, a company may claim a deduction of 2.5 times the amount donated to an approved Institution of a Public Character (IPC) or the Singapore Government to benefit the local community. The company must provide its UEN to the approved IPC. IRAS says approved donation amounts are pre-filled in Form C-S, Form C-S (Lite) or Form C based on information obtained from IPCs. In the tax computation, add back all donations, then deduct 2.5 times approved donations; the deduction is on a preceding-financial-year basis. The 2.5-times deduction applies to donations made from 1 January 2016 through 31 December 2029 under the captured current guidance. The donee must be an approved IPC or the Singapore Government, and a Government donation must benefit the local community. For an IPC donation, the company must provide its UEN to the IPC to receive the deduction. Approved donations are considered on a preceding-financial-year basis. Donations outside the approved-donation category remain non-deductible business expenses under this cited rule. This record does not cover individual income-tax donations, other incentive schemes, tax-exemption computation, or whether a named donee is currently approved. For case-specific application, consider: Donation date and financial year. Donee identity and current approved-IPC status, or whether a Singapore Government donation benefits the local community. Donation amount and the amount recorded by IRAS; whether the company provided its UEN to the IPC. This guidance does not calculate the company’s adjusted profit, chargeable income or tax deduction amount. Confirm that the donee and donation are eligible and reconcile the amount with the applicable YA before filing. [IRAS | Tax Treatment of Business Expenses (A-F)](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/income-deductions-for-companies/business-expenses/tax-treatment-of-business-expenses-(a-f))

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**IRAS company income-tax record retention and responsible person** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A company must retain source documents, accounting records and schedules, bank statements and other transaction-connected business records for at least five years from the relevant Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS gives examples: records for YA 2019 are retained to 31 December 2023, while records for YA 2023 are retained to 31 December 2027. For a company struck off and dissolved, the officer immediately before dissolution keeps the books and papers for at least five years after dissolution; for a wound-up company, the liquidator does so for at least five years from dissolution. Use the relevant YA for ordinary company tax records; the page’s examples distinguish December and non-December financial-year ends. After dissolution, the source identifies a different responsible person and starts the five-year period from dissolution. This is corporate income tax record guidance, not the separate GST record-retention rule. The ordinary YA period does not replace the separate dissolution-date duties for struck-off or wound-up companies. For case-specific application, consider: The relevant YA and financial-year period. Whether the company was struck off and dissolved or wound up, and its dissolution date. The source examples explain ordinary YA retention; they do not determine every record-specific retention requirement. A company-specific last-retention date requires the correct YA or dissolution date. For YA 2023, retain the records through at least 31 December 2027. rows.before:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF Ordinary Wage versus Additional Wage classification by employment month and payable date** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** The stated salary is for employment in March, but is payable on 20 April, after the 14th of the following month. It therefore is not March OW and is classified as AW for that month. AW may still attract CPF, subject to its applicable annual ceiling and contribution rate; the pay-period label alone does not make it OW. [CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/what-constitutes-wages-for-cpf-contributions)

**Source:** CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF Ordinary Wage versus Additional Wage classification by employment month and payable date): Under the CPF Act, wages are defined as remuneration in money, including any bonus that is due or granted to a person in respect of his employment.

Only payments that are considered wages should be included when declaring wage information and computing CPF contributions.

Payments to include as wages

Basic wage: Salary payable to an employee for work done.
Overtime pay: Payment to an employee for working beyond normal working hours.
Bonus: Payment such as performance bonus.
Allowance: For example, meal allowance and transport allowance.
Commission: For example, sales commission.
Cash incentive: For example, productivity incentive.

Payments not to include as wages

Termination benefit: Compensation that is not given for services or work done by the employee. For example, retrenchment benefit.
Reimbursement: Reimbursement incurred on behalf of the employer for official purposes. The reimbursement amount must not exceed the expenditure incurred. For example, purchase of office stationery.
Benefit in kind: Non-cash benefit or gift given to the employee. For example, a commemorative watch.

Classifying wages as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages

After determining that a payment is wages, classify it correctly as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages. The wage type affects how CPF contributions are computed and how the wage information should be declared.

Total Wages is the sum of Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. CPF contributions are computed on the Total Wages payable to an employee in a calendar month, subject to the applicable Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings.

For wages to be classified as Ordinary Wages for the month, they must meet both of the following conditions:

* They are given to an employee for their employment in that month; and
* They are payable by the 14th of the following month.

For example, monthly salary.

Wages which are not classified as Ordinary Wages will be Additional Wages for the month.

For example, annual performance bonus.

The Additional Wage ceiling sets the maximum amount of AW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar year for all employees. It is applied on a per employee, per employer, per calendar year basis.

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF newly obtained PR status and OW/AW payable-date treatment): As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF newly obtained PR status and OW/AW payable-date treatment): Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

Current rates

Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)

Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM sick and hospitalisation leave eligibility and entitlement** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee with at least 3 months’ service who informs, or tries to inform, the employer within 48 hours may qualify for paid outpatient sick and hospitalisation leave on the applicable medical certification. The example entitlement is 5 days of outpatient sick leave and 15 days of hospitalisation leave at month 3; 8 outpatient and 30 hospitalisation days at month 4; 11 outpatient and 45 hospitalisation days at month 5; and from month 6, 14 days of outpatient leave and 60 days of hospitalisation leave. The 60-day hospitalisation cap includes outpatient leave. The Employment Act applies, at least 3 months of service are completed, and the employer is notified or attempted to be notified within 48 hours. Outpatient leave requires a registered medical or dental practitioner’s certification. Hospitalisation leave must meet the specified care/quarantine conditions and certification requirements. The 60 hospitalisation days include the 14 outpatient days; they are not 60 days in addition to outpatient leave. Historical table application is not established by this current page. Cosmetic procedures are not required paid sick leave under the page. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act coverage, employment start date and service months completed. When the employer was informed, qualifying medical certificate and whether care satisfies the hospitalisation definition. Outpatient and hospitalisation leave already taken in the relevant entitlement year. General entitlement only; case eligibility and remaining balance require the listed employee, notice, certification and leave-use facts. Time off in lieu (only for employees not covered under Part 4 of Employment Act).

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA small-company audit exemption criteria** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** Small-company audit exemption requires the entity to be a private company in the financial year and to meet at least two of the three quantitative criteria for each of the immediate past two consecutive financial years: revenue no more than S$10 million, assets no more than S$10 million, or no more than 50 full-time employees at FYE. A company that is less than two years old is assessed against criteria in its current year. A group also has to meet the separate consolidated small-group criteria. Two of three criteria must hold for both immediately preceding consecutive financial years for an established company; “this year and last year” does not always establish that period. The Singapore company and the entire group (including foreign entities) must each satisfy their respective test where the company is part of a group. A qualifying company remains qualified until it ceases to be private or no longer meets at least two criteria over the immediate past two consecutive financial years. The current-year test applies to a newly incorporated private company less than two years old. A separate dormant-company audit exemption may apply; do not confuse audit exemption with relief from preparing financial statements or filing an annual return. A case-specific conclusion requires: Private-company status during the financial year. Revenue, total assets and full-time employee count for the immediate past two consecutive financial years. If part of a group, the consolidated figures and entire-group scope. Whether the company is newly incorporated or another audit exception is being considered. A company-specific conclusion needs two financial years’ facts and, for a group, consolidated facts. Audit exemption does not exempt a company from keeping proper records, preparing financial statements, annual-return filing or tax filing. [Audit exemptions: Small company concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/preparing-financial-statements/audit-exemptions/)

**Source:** Audit exemptions: Small company concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA small-company audit exemption criteria): Learn when your private company qualifies for audit exemption under the small company concept. This exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.

To qualify for audit exemption as a small company, you need to meet both of these criteria:

•

• Your company is a private company in the financial year; and

•

•

• Your company meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:

•

◦

◦ Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ 50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year

◦

•

If your company is newly incorporated (less than two years old)

You qualify for audit exemption if you meet the criteria in the current financial year.

Example:

•

• First financial year: Check if you are a private company and meet two out of three quantitative criteria that year.

•

•

• Second financial year: If you did not qualify in the first year, check again using the same requirements for the second year.

•

If your company is part of a group

You need to meet both of these conditions to qualify for audit exemption:

•

• Your Singapore company or subsidiary qualifies as a small company; and

•

•

• Your entire group (including foreign entities) meets at least two of these quantitative criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years:

•

◦

◦ Total annual revenue of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ Total assets of $10 million or less, based on your holding company's consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting standards

◦

•

◦

◦ 50 employees or fewer, based on the number of full-time employees at the end of your financial year

◦

•

Note: The audit exemption applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 July 2015.

Maintaining your exemption status

Once your company qualifies as a small company, you remain qualified in subsequent financial years unless:

•

• You cease to be a private company at any time during a financial year; or

•

•

• You do not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years

•

Once your group qualifies as a small group, it remains qualified for subsequent financial years. This applies until it does not meet at least two out of three criteria for the immediate past two consecutive financial years.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Yes, you can qualify for audit exemption even if you have corporate shareholders.

Unlike the previous criteria, you do not need to be an exempt private company to qualify for audit exemption.

No, it does not change your financial statement filing requirements.

Yes, audit exemption is for private companies.

Section 205B of the Companies Act exempts a dormant company from audit requirements. A dormant company is not limited to a private company.

Section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act exempts a small company from audit requirements. This exemption is only applicable to private companies.

In deciding whether a company should be treated as a small company or a small group for the purpose of being exempted from audit requirements, the company would need to refer to section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act. In particular, para 12(a) of the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act states that “the question whether an entity is part of a group is to be decided in accordance with the Accounting Standards”.

If the company is owned by another company (i.e. parent company), it will need to assess whether it belongs to a small group, regardless of whether it prepares and/or file consolidated financial statements.

The assessment will be based on the past two years financials.

On whether a company is a small company or a small group for the purpose of being exempted from audit requirements, the company would have to refer to section 205C read with the Thirteenth Schedule of the Companies Act. In particular paras. 7, 8 and 9 of the Thirteenth Schedule set out the situations in which the criteria for audit exemption should be applied to the first financial year of consolidation or the two financial years preceding the financial year of consolidation.
- Official source: [Audit exemptions: Small company concept | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/manage/companies/legal-requirements-common-offences/preparing-financial-statements/audit-exemptions/)

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA company secretary appointment and sole-director requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s guide says every company must have a company secretary, appointed within six months of successful registration, and the position cannot remain vacant for more than six months. The director may face a fine of up to S$1,000 if the vacancy exceeds that period. The guide says the secretary must be a real person who is a Singapore citizen, permanent resident, or otherwise meets the local residency rules; the sole director cannot also be the company secretary. The secretary’s administrative role includes maintaining company information and registers, organising and recording meetings, reminding directors of annual filing deadlines, and updating them on new rules. This overview is not a complete statutory eligibility check: verify the Companies Act requirements for residence, non-debarment and knowledge or experience, plus any additional public-company qualifications, before concluding that a candidate qualifies. A secretary must be appointed within six months of successful registration. The position cannot be empty for more than six months. Otherwise, the director may face a fine of up to $1,000.

Directors run the company and decide on its strategy and direction.

Under the Companies Act, company directors must:

•

• Be ordinarily resident

•

•

• Be 18 years old or older

•

•

• Be mentally fit to make decisions

•

•

• Be a Singapore citizen, Singapore permanent resident, or someone who meets local residency rules

•

•

• Not be banned from being a director

•

•

• Not be disqualified from acting as a director of a company (for example, an undischarged bankrupt)

•

Note: If you are a Foreign Identification Number (FIN) holder, check with your pass issuer (such as Ministry of Manpower (MOM) (opens in new tab) or Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) (opens in new tab)) before you accept a role.

All company directors have a key duty to follow the Companies Act.

Duties and penalties

What you need to know

Details

•

• Keep proper records

•

•

• Prepare financial reports (when needed)

•

•

• File required documents with ACRA on time

•

•

• Act in the company's best interests

•

Note: You cannot be an “inactive director”, “nominee director”, or “sleeping director”. All directors are responsible under the legislation, whether active or not.

Penalties

Directors who do not meet these duties may face penalties. Depending on severity, these may include:

•

• Fines up to $5,000

•

•

• Up to two years in jail

•

•

• Being banned from being a director for five years

•

New directors can take a free Directors Training Programme. The two-hour course covers:

•

• Director requirements

•

•

• Your key duties and responsibilities under the Companies Act

•

•

• Tax filing information

•

•

• Employee Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions

•

•

• Workplace safety rules

•

Tip: This programme also includes important information from other government agencies.

Nominee directors act as directors for your company, but represent another person or entity. This happens when the director is required (formally or informally) to follow the directions, instructions, or wishes of another person. The person or entity they represent is called the nominator.

On the date of your company's incorporation, the nominee director needs to:

•

• Inform the company that they are a nominee director.

•

•

• Provide the nominator's details.

•

Company secretaries help the company to comply with its requirements.

A company secretary must:

•

• Be a real person (not a company)

•

•

• Be a Singapore citizen, Singapore permanent resident, or someone who meets local residency rules

•

•

• Not be the same person as the sole director

•

Company secretaries handle administrative work, including:

•

• Maintaining their local company's information and registers or maintaining their foreign company's information

•

•

• Organising meetings and taking notes

•

•

• Reminding directors about annual filing deadlines

•

•

• Updating everyone on any new rules

**VCFM Form 7 cessation and noncommencement notification** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** A VCFM must submit Form 7, Notice of Cessation of Business, if it ceases to carry on any or all regulated activities. For cessation, the toolkit says to notify MAS within 14 days after the cessation and accompany Form 7 with an audit certification, in no prescribed format, that the VCFM has fully discharged all customer obligations. A VCFM that has not commenced any or all regulated activities by the end of six months from the CMS licence grant must submit Form 7 immediately after that six-month period ends. Whether the event is cessation or non-commencement, the regulated activity affected, and the cessation date or CMS licence grant date.
